description: Quantitative Foundations: probability, statistical inference, regression and GLMs, causal inference, Bayesian methods, machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, queueing, linear algebra and information theory, with geometric intuitions. For an engineer/architect who reads papers, sizes systems and judges evidence.

notes.front: What is the classic confusion with conditional probability \(P(A\mid B)\)?
notes.back: Treating \(P(A\mid B)\) as if it were \(P(B\mid A)\) (the prosecutor's fallacy).
notes.extra: Example: P(error log contains 'timeout' | database is down) may be 95%. P(database is down | log contains 'timeout') may be 5%, because timeouts have many other causes.

notes.front: What does it mean for events A and B to be independent?
notes.back: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)\): knowing one tells you nothing about the other.

notes.front: Why does wrongly assuming independent failures break reliability math?
notes.back: Shared causes (power supply, firmware, rack) correlate failures, so "multiply the small probabilities" is wildly optimistic.
notes.extra: Example: two disks each fail 1%/year. Independent: both fail ≈ 0.01%. Sharing a power supply or firmware bug: closer to 1%. RAID math assumes independence that rarely holds.

notes.front: Why can expected value mislead?
notes.back: \(E[X]=\sum x\,P(x)\) is a long-run average per trial, not a typical outcome; rare huge values dominate it.
notes.extra: Example: A lottery ticket costs €2 and has expected value €1. Playing once, you almost surely lose €2. A service with mean latency 50 ms can have most requests at 10 ms and a few at 5 s.

notes.front: Why report the standard deviation rather than the variance?
notes.back: \(\sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}}\) is in the same units as X, so it is interpretable; the variance \(E[(X-\mu)^2]\) is in squared units.
notes.extra: Example: Two API endpoints both average 100 ms. One has σ = 5 ms (predictable), the other σ = 200 ms (a lottery). Same mean, completely different user experience and capacity needs.

notes.text: Finite-variance random variables form the Hilbert space \(L^2\) with \(\langle X,Y\rangle=E[XY]\). For centred variables: length = {{c1::standard deviation}}, inner product = {{c2::covariance}}, orthogonal = {{c3::uncorrelated}}.
notes.extra: Geometry: Every second-moment fact in statistics is Euclidean geometry in this space: lengths are standard deviations, angles are correlations, "best predictor" means "orthogonal projection". Most of regression is Pythagoras in disguise.

notes.front: What is the geometric meaning of the Pearson correlation \(\rho(X,Y)\)?
notes.back: \(\rho=\cos\theta\): the cosine of the angle between the centred variables (in a sample, between the centred data vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\rho=1\): parallel. \(\rho=0\): perpendicular. \(\rho=-1\): anti-parallel. This is why \(|\rho|\le 1\) is just Cauchy-Schwarz, and why correlation is not transitive: A can be at 45° to B and B at 45° to C while A is at 90° to C.

notes.front: \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\) is which geometric theorem?
notes.back: The law of cosines; for uncorrelated variables (90° apart) it reduces to Pythagoras.
notes.analogy: Standard deviations add like the sides of a triangle, not like numbers.

notes.front: Geometrically, why does the standard error of a mean shrink as \(1/\sqrt{n}\)?
notes.back: Independent errors add at right angles: n errors of size σ sum to length \(\sigma\sqrt n\) (the diagonal of an n-dimensional box). Dividing by n gives \(\sigma/\sqrt n\).

notes.front: Geometrically, what is the conditional expectation \(E[Y\mid X]\)?
notes.back: The orthogonal projection of Y onto the subspace of all (square-integrable) functions of X: it minimises \(E[(Y-g(X))^2]\), and the error is orthogonal to every function of X.
notes.extra: Geometry: Linear regression projects onto the small subspace spanned by linear functions of \(X\); conditional expectation projects onto the much larger subspace of all functions of \(X\). The tower property \(E[E[Y|X,Z]\,|\,X]=E[Y|X]\) is just "projecting onto a subspace of a subspace in two steps equals projecting once".

notes.text: Law of total variance: \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\) {{c1::\(\mathrm{Var}(E[Y\mid X])\)}} (explained) + {{c2::\(E[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]\)}} (unexplained).
notes.extra: Geometry: Pythagoras. \(Y - E[Y]\) is the hypotenuse; the projection \(E[Y|X]-E[Y]\) and the residual \(Y-E[Y|X]\) are the perpendicular legs. \(R^2\) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) are both this single right triangle.

notes.front: What shape does a covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) describe, and what do its eigenvectors and eigenvalues mean?
notes.back: Its level sets are ellipsoids. Eigenvectors are the principal axes; \(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\) are the semi-axis lengths (standard deviations along those axes).
notes.extra: Geometry: \(\Sigma^{1/2}\) is the linear map that turns the unit sphere (white noise) into this ellipsoid. Every multivariate Gaussian is a rotated, stretched, shifted spherical Gaussian.

notes.front: What does the Mahalanobis distance measure?
notes.back: \(\sqrt{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}\): Euclidean distance after whitening, i.e. distance in standard deviations along each principal axis.
notes.analogy: Squash the covariance ellipse back into a circle, then use an ordinary ruler: a point far out along the long axis is less surprising than one equally far along the short axis.
notes.extra: In practice: a natural multivariate anomaly score.

notes.front: For a joint Gaussian \((x_1,x_2)\), what is \(E[x_1\mid x_2]\)?
notes.back: \(\mu_1+\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(x_2-\mu_2)\): linear in \(x_2\), exactly the regression formula.

notes.front: For a joint Gaussian, what is remarkable about \(\mathrm{Cov}[x_1\mid x_2]\)?
notes.back: It is the Schur complement \(\Sigma_{11}-\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\), which does not depend on the observed value \(x_2\).
notes.extra: Geometry: Conditioning = slicing the ellipsoid with a plane \(x_2 = \text{const}\). Every parallel slice of an ellipsoid is the same ellipse shape, just shifted along a straight line: hence constant covariance and linear mean.

notes.front: Geometrically, how do marginalising and conditioning a multivariate Gaussian differ?
notes.back: Marginalising = projecting (a shadow): drop rows/columns of \(\Sigma\). Conditioning = slicing: drop rows/columns of the precision \(\Lambda=\Sigma^{-1}\). A shadow is wider than any slice.

notes.front: In a Gaussian, what does a zero in \(\Sigma\) mean vs a zero in the precision matrix \(\Lambda\)?
notes.back: Zero in \(\Sigma\): marginal independence. Zero in \(\Lambda\): conditional independence given the rest (the basis of Gaussian graphical models).

notes.front: What does the Law of Large Numbers say, and what does it not say?
notes.back: The sample mean converges to the true mean as n grows. It does not say deviations "even out" in the short run (gambler's fallacy), nor how fast convergence is for heavy-tailed data.
notes.extra: Example: After 10 heads in a row, the next flip is still 50/50. The average tends to 0.5 by drowning the 10 heads in thousands of later flips, not by producing extra tails.

notes.front: What does the Central Limit Theorem state?
notes.back: For i.i.d. variables with mean μ and finite variance σ², \(\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2)\): sums and means are approximately normal whatever the individual distribution.

notes.front: What is the practical consequence of the CLT, and when does it fail?
notes.back: Error bars on averages work even for skewed data (e.g. daily mean latency over a million requests). It needs finite variance, so it silently fails for power-law data.

notes.front: Why is the Gaussian the limit in the CLT?
notes.back: Adding independent variables convolves their densities; the Gaussian is the fixed point of "convolve and rescale" and the maximum-entropy distribution for a given variance.
notes.analogy: Convolution is repeated blurring: blur any shape often enough and all detail except location and width is erased.

notes.front: Bernoulli vs Binomial distribution?
notes.back: Bernoulli: one yes/no trial with success probability p. Binomial(n, p): number of successes in n independent trials; mean np, variance np(1−p).
notes.extra: Example: Each of 500 hosts has a 2% chance of failing a health check. Failures ~ Binomial(500, 0.02): mean 10, σ ≈ 3.1. Seeing 25 failures is ~5σ—something systemic is happening.

notes.front: What does the Poisson distribution model, and what is its key property?
notes.back: Counts of independent events in a fixed interval at a constant average rate λ. Mean = variance = λ.
notes.extra: Example: A service gets 100 requests/s on average. In any given second, P(≥130 requests) ≈ 0.2%—so a fixed capacity of 130 rps will be exceeded in roughly 1 second out of every 500, even with no traffic spike. Good default for arrivals, errors and defects.

notes.front: What does the exponential distribution model, and what is memorylessness?
notes.back: Waiting time between Poisson events (mean 1/λ). Memoryless: \(P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=P(T>t)\): time already waited tells you nothing.
notes.extra: Example: If bus arrivals were truly Poisson, having waited 20 minutes already would not make the bus 'due'. Real buses are scheduled, so they are not memoryless; radioactive decay and many failure processes are.

notes.front: When is a normal model reasonable, and when is it a trap?
notes.back: Reasonable for sums of many small independent effects (measurement noise, sample means). A trap for quantities bounded at zero, multiplicative, or driven by rare large events: latency, file sizes, outage cost.
notes.extra: Example: Modeling latency as normal with mean 100 ms and σ 50 ms implies negative latencies and a p99.9 of ~250 ms. Real p99.9 might be 3 s.

notes.front: What generates a log-normal distribution, and how do you recognise it?
notes.back: A product of many positive random factors (its log is a sum, hence normal). Right-skewed with a long tail; looks normal on a log axis. Common for latency and response sizes.
notes.extra: Example: Request latency = network × queueing × DB × serialization, each a multiplicative slowdown. The result is log-normal-ish: median 40 ms, mean 70 ms, p99 500 ms.

notes.front: Why is the mean useless for heavy-tailed (power-law) data?
notes.back: Tails decay polynomially, so extremes aren't rare: the sample mean is dominated by the largest observation and may not converge; variance can be infinite. Plan for the tail.
notes.extra: Example: Cascading-failure cost, file sizes on a shared drive, follower counts. 'Average outage cost' is meaningless when one outage per decade dwarfs all others combined. Plan for the tail, not the mean.

notes.front: Why report percentiles (p50, p99) rather than the mean for latency?
notes.back: Percentiles describe the distribution's shape, including the tail; the mean hides tails and can be dominated by a few huge values.

notes.front: State Jensen's inequality and its picture.
notes.back: For convex f: \(f(E[X])\le E[f(X)]\). Picture: a chord of a convex function lies above the curve.
notes.extra: Underlies: KL ≥ 0, the ELBO, \(E[X^2]\ge E[X]^2\), and why the log of an average exceeds the average of logs.

notes.front: Where does the probability mass of a d-dimensional standard Gaussian live when d is large?
notes.back: In a thin shell of radius ≈ \(\sqrt d\), not near the mode at the origin, even though density is highest there.
notes.analogy: A high-dimensional Gaussian is a soap bubble, not a ball.
notes.extra: Geometry: mass = density × volume. Density falls as \(e^{-r^2/2}\) but shell volume grows as \(r^{d-1}\); the product peaks sharply at \(r\approx\sqrt{d-1}\). This shell is the "typical set".

notes.text: Curse of dimensionality: {{c1::volume concentrates near the surface}} (the outer ε-shell holds \(1-(1-\epsilon)^d\to1\)); {{c2::distances concentrate}} (nearest ≈ farthest neighbour); {{c3::random vectors are nearly orthogonal}} (\(\cos\theta\sim N(0,1/d)\)).

notes.front: Why do "local" methods (kNN, kernel smoothing) break down in high dimensions?
notes.back: To capture 10% of a unit hypercube in 10-D, a sub-cube needs side \(0.1^{1/10}\approx0.8\): "local" spans 80% of every axis. Keeping neighbourhoods local needs data exponential in d.
notes.extra: The rescue: real data lies near low-dimensional manifolds.

notes.front: What is one bit of information, in Shannon's sense?
notes.back: The information that halves your uncertainty: the answer to one fair yes/no question. An event of probability p carries \(-\log_2 p\) bits of surprise.
notes.extra: Example: Learning a fair coin landed heads: 1 bit. Learning a die showed 4: log₂ 6 ≈ 2.58 bits. Learning the sun rose: ≈ 0 bits, you already knew. A 1-in-a-million event: ~20 bits.

notes.front: Define entropy H(X) and give its intuition.
notes.back: \(H(X)=-\sum p(x)\log_2p(x)\): the average surprise per outcome, i.e. how unpredictable the source is. Maximal for a uniform distribution, zero for a certain outcome.
notes.extra: Example: Fair coin: 1 bit. Coin that lands heads 99% of the time: 0.08 bits—almost nothing to learn from each flip. A log line that is always 'OK' has zero entropy; a log with rich variety has high entropy.

notes.front: What does Shannon's source-coding theorem say?
notes.back: Entropy is the minimum average number of bits per symbol for any lossless code: you can approach it but never beat it.
notes.extra: Example: English text has ~1–1.5 bits of entropy per character but is stored at 8 bits/char. That ~6× redundancy is what gzip exploits. A file of random bytes has 8 bits/byte entropy: gzip cannot shrink it, and 'compressing' it makes it slightly larger.

notes.front: What is the idea of Huffman coding?
notes.back: Repeatedly merge the two least-probable symbols into a tree, so frequent symbols get short codes; optimal code length ≈ \(-\log_2p(x)\).
notes.analogy: Morse code by hand: the commonest letter "E" is a single dot, rare "Q" is dash-dash-dot-dash.

notes.front: Define cross-entropy \(H(p,q)\).
notes.back: \(-\sum p(x)\log q(x)\): the average bits needed to encode data from the true distribution p using a code optimised for q. Minimised when q = p.

notes.front: How do cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence relate?
notes.back: \(H(p,q)=H(p)+\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)\). H(p) doesn't depend on the model, so minimising cross-entropy = minimising KL = maximising likelihood.
notes.analogy: H(p) is the irreducible length of the trip over the terrain; KL is the detour caused by a wrong map. Training can only shrink the detour.

notes.front: Define KL divergence and what it measures.
notes.back: \(\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)=E_p[\log(p/q)]\ge0\): the extra bits (log-loss) wasted by using model q when the truth is p.
notes.extra: Example: RLHF keeps a KL penalty between the tuned and base model: improve the reward without drifting far from what you were.

notes.front: Why isn't KL divergence a true distance?
notes.back: It is asymmetric (\(\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\ne\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\)) and violates the triangle inequality.
notes.extra: Geometry: Locally it behaves like a squared distance: \(\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+d\theta}) \approx \tfrac12\, d\theta^\top I(\theta)\, d\theta\) with \(I\) the Fisher information. So the Fisher information is the metric tensor of the curved "statistical manifold" and KL is its (asymmetric) squared-length surrogate.

notes.front: What does mutual information I(X;Y) measure, and why is it better than correlation?
notes.back: \(H(X)-H(X\mid Y)\): how many bits Y tells you about X; zero iff independent. Unlike correlation it captures any dependence (nonlinear, non-monotonic, categorical).
notes.extra: Example: Y = X² for X in [−1, 1] has correlation 0 but high mutual information. Feature selection by mutual information catches features correlation-based filters miss.

notes.front: What is perplexity, and how do you read it?
notes.back: \(2^{\text{cross-entropy (bits)}}\): the effective number of equally likely tokens the model is choosing between. Perplexity 20 = as uncertain as a uniform pick among 20.

notes.front: Why is "compression is prediction" literally true?
notes.back: A predictor assigning probability q(x) can encode x in \(-\log_2q(x)\) bits (arithmetic coding), and any compressor implies a predictor. An LLM's cross-entropy loss is its compression rate.
notes.extra: Example: A trained LLM compresses text far better than gzip because it 'knows' that after 'the capital of France is' the next token is nearly certain. Its loss in bits/token is exactly its compression rate.

notes.front: Why is randomness incompressible, and what does that let you detect?
notes.back: A truly random sequence has no description shorter than itself (Kolmogorov complexity ≈ length). So compressibility tests for structure: if gzip shrinks "random" session IDs, the generator is flawed.
notes.extra: Example: a 1 GB file gzip can't shrink is already compressed, encrypted, or noise.

notes.front: What does the noisy-channel coding theorem say?
notes.back: Every noisy channel has a capacity C. Below C you can transmit with arbitrarily low error using clever error-correcting codes; above C you cannot.
notes.analogy: Reliability comes from cleverly structured redundancy, not from shouting louder.

notes.front: Shannon–Hartley: why does Wi-Fi get faster with wider channels rather than more power?
notes.back: \(C=B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR})\): capacity is linear in bandwidth B but only logarithmic in signal power. Doubling power adds only ~1 bit/s per Hz.

notes.front: What does the maximum-entropy principle say?
notes.back: Among all distributions consistent with your constraints, pick the one with the highest entropy: it assumes nothing extra.
notes.extra: Example: if all you know about latency is its mean, the least-assuming model is exponential; a Gaussian smuggles in symmetry and thin tails.

notes.text: Maximum-entropy distributions: fixed support [a,b] only → {{c1::uniform}}; fixed mean on \([0,\infty)\) → {{c2::exponential}}; fixed mean and variance on ℝ → {{c3::Gaussian}}; constraints on \(E[T(x)]\) in general → the {{c4::exponential family}}.
notes.extra: Geometry: maximum entropy = the flattest, least committal distribution compatible with what you know; the constraints' Lagrange multipliers become the natural parameters.

notes.front: How do you compute password or key entropy, and what is the trap?
notes.back: \(\log_2\)(number of equally likely possibilities the attacker must search). Trap: entropy belongs to the generating process, not the string; human "complex" passwords come from a small, predictable set.
notes.extra: Example: 4 random words from a 7,776-word list ≈ 51.7 bits. "P@ssw0rd2024!" is in every cracking dictionary. A 128-bit key: \(2^{128}\approx3.4\times10^{38}\) tries.

notes.front: What does Minimum Description Length (MDL) say?
notes.back: The best model minimises (bits to describe the model) + (bits to describe the data given the model). A perfect but enormous fit has explained nothing.
notes.analogy: Occam's razor priced in bits.
notes.extra: Example: A 200-parameter polynomial through 200 points has zero error but costs 200 numbers to state: it has memorized, not compressed. A line with small noise costs 2 numbers plus cheap residuals—that is the real pattern.

notes.front: In ML papers, what is a vector?
notes.back: An ordered list of numbers representing a point or direction in n-dimensional space: an embedding, an image's pixels, a user's feature row, a model's parameters.

notes.front: What does the dot product measure geometrically?
notes.back: \(a\cdot b=\sum a_ib_i=|a||b|\cos\theta\): alignment. Large when pointing the same way, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposed.

notes.front: Why is the dot product everywhere in ML?
notes.back: Every neuron computes inputs · weights; attention scores are query · key; cosine similarity (dot product of unit vectors) powers semantic search.

notes.front: What does multiplying a vector by a matrix do?
notes.back: Applies a linear map: rotate, scale, shear or project, never bend. \(Ax\) combines A's columns using x's entries as weights.

notes.front: Why is matrix multiplication defined the way it is?
notes.back: AB is the composition "apply B, then A", defined so that \((AB)x=A(Bx)\). Inner dimensions must match, and order matters (rotate-then-stretch ≠ stretch-then-rotate).

notes.front: Why is a deep network without nonlinearities no better than a single layer?
notes.back: \(W_3W_2W_1x\) collapses to one matrix \(W=W_3W_2W_1\). Nonlinear activations between layers are what make depth matter.

notes.front: When does a matrix inverse \(A^{-1}\) exist, intuitively?
notes.back: Only if A loses no information: square and full rank. A projection onto a plane has no inverse, because the flattened dimension is gone.
notes.extra: Solving \(Ax=b\) is "undo A", which is why a singular A means no unique solution. (\(A^\top\) swaps rows and columns; \(x^\top y\) is the dot product.)

notes.front: What is the rank of a matrix intuitively, and what does "low-rank" mean?
notes.back: Rank = number of independent directions the output can span = the map's true dimensionality. Low-rank: mostly redundant, writable as a product of two thin matrices.
notes.extra: Example: LoRA learns \(\Delta W=AB\) with A d×8 and B 8×d instead of a full d×d update, betting that the needed change is low-rank.

notes.front: What are eigenvectors and eigenvalues, intuitively?
notes.back: \(Av=\lambda v\): directions the map only stretches (by λ), never rotates. They are the map's natural axes; eigenvalues say how much each axis is amplified or damped.

notes.front: What happens when you apply the same matrix to a vector over and over?
notes.back: The eigen-direction with the largest |λ| is amplified until it dominates: power iteration, which is how PageRank (the leading eigenvector of the link matrix) is computed.

notes.front: What does the SVD \(A=U\Sigma V^\top\) say geometrically?
notes.back: Every linear map = rotate/reflect (\(V^\top\)), stretch along the axes (Σ), rotate/reflect (U). The unit sphere maps to an ellipsoid with semi-axes \(\sigma_iu_i\). Works for non-square matrices.

notes.front: What do the singular values of a matrix tell you?
notes.back: Rank = number of non-zero \(\sigma_i\); condition number = \(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\); truncating the small ones gives the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young).
notes.extra: Example: keep the top 50 singular values of a sparse users × items rating matrix: every user and item becomes a 50-dim vector whose dot product predicts ratings (a recommender). Near-zero singular values cause ill-conditioning in regression.

notes.front: L1 vs L2 norm: definitions and the shapes of their unit balls?
notes.back: L2 (Euclidean) \(\sqrt{\sum x_i^2}\): a round ball. L1 (Manhattan) \(\sum|x_i|\): a diamond with corners on the axes.

notes.front: What does softmax do?
notes.back: \(\mathrm{softmax}(z)_i=e^{z_i}/\sum_je^{z_j}\) turns arbitrary scores into a probability distribution, exaggerating differences so the largest score takes most of the mass.
notes.extra: Example: logits [2, 1, 0] → [0.67, 0.24, 0.09]. Adding a constant to all logits changes nothing.

notes.front: What does dividing logits by a temperature T do to a softmax?
notes.back: T → 0 sharpens toward argmax (one-hot); T → ∞ flattens toward uniform. LLM sampling temperature is exactly this knob.
notes.extra: Geometry: softmax maps logits onto the probability simplex; low T pushes toward a vertex, high T toward the centroid.

notes.front: What does a derivative dy/dx tell you, in plain language?
notes.back: Sensitivity: nudge x by ε and y moves by about (dy/dx)·ε. It is the slope of the local linear approximation.
notes.extra: Example: d(loss)/dw = −3 means increasing w slightly lowers the loss, so move w up. That sentence is gradient descent.

notes.front: What is the key geometric fact about the gradient ∇f?
notes.back: It points in the direction of steepest ascent, with magnitude = the slope in that direction, and is perpendicular to level sets. −∇f is steepest descent.
notes.analogy: Standing blindfolded on a hillside: the gradient is the direction your feet feel the ground rising fastest.

notes.front: Why is the chain rule the whole of backpropagation?
notes.back: \(\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\): sensitivities multiply along a chain. A network is a long chain of functions, so any weight's gradient is a product of local derivatives from that weight to the loss.

notes.front: What is a Jacobian, and where do you meet it?
notes.back: The matrix of all first partial derivatives of a vector-valued \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), its best linear approximation. Backpropagation multiplies Jacobians.

notes.front: What is a Hessian, and what do its eigenvalues tell you at a critical point?
notes.back: The matrix of second partials of a scalar function (its curvature). All eigenvalues positive: minimum; all negative: maximum; mixed signs: saddle.
notes.extra: Second-order optimisers (Newton) use it. A "sharp" minimum has large eigenvalues and is said to generalise worse than a flat one.

notes.front: What is a convex function, and why does it matter for optimisation?
notes.back: Its graph lies below every chord (bowl-shaped), so every local minimum is global and a zero gradient certifies the optimum.
notes.analogy: A convex loss is one valley: a ball rolled from anywhere ends at the bottom. A non-convex loss is a mountain range: where you start decides which valley you reach (why random seeds change deep-learning results).
notes.extra: Least squares, logistic and hinge losses (with L1/L2 penalties) are convex; deep networks are not.

notes.front: Two equivalent tests for convexity of a smooth function?
notes.back: Tangent planes lie below the graph, \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\); or (twice differentiable) the Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere.
notes.extra: Geometry: because a tangent plane is a global lower bound, a zero gradient certifies a global minimum.

notes.front: How do integrals show up in probability?
notes.back: Integrating a density over a region gives probability, \(P(a<X<b)=\int_a^bp(x)\,dx\); integrating value × density gives an average, \(E[g(X)]=\int g(x)p(x)\,dx\).
notes.extra: Example: the marginal likelihood \(P(E)=\int P(E\mid\theta)P(\theta)\,d\theta\) sums over all parameter values, weighted by plausibility.

notes.front: Why does the Taylor expansion appear in optimisation?
notes.back: \(f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+f'(x)\delta+\tfrac12f''(x)\delta^2\). The first-order term justifies gradient descent; the second-order (Hessian) term justifies Newton's method.

notes.front: Via Taylor, why does too high a learning rate make the loss go up?
notes.back: If the step \(\delta=-\eta g\) is so large that the curvature term \(\tfrac12\delta^\top H\delta\) outweighs the linear gain \(g\cdot\delta\), the loss increases: divergence.

notes.front: State Little's Law.
notes.back: \(L=\lambda W\): average items in the system = arrival (throughput) rate × average time in the system. Holds for any stable system, whatever the arrival or service distributions.
notes.analogy: A coffee shop serving 60 customers/hour, each staying 10 minutes, has on average 60 × 1/6 = 10 customers inside.

notes.front: Little's Law: size the connection pool for 1,000 requests/s at 50 ms average latency.
notes.back: Concurrency = λW = 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 requests in flight. A pool of 40 will queue; 500 wastes memory.

notes.front: Why do connection pools exhaust in cascades when a dependency slows down?
notes.back: Needed concurrency = throughput × latency: if latency doubles at the same throughput, the required pool size doubles too.

notes.front: A Kafka consumer group has a stable backlog of 200,000 messages and processes 5,000 msg/s. How long does each message wait?
notes.back: \(W=L/\lambda=200{,}000/5{,}000=\) 40 s, with no timestamps needed.
notes.extra: Same trick: 30 open tickets, 5 closed per week → 6 weeks average cycle time.

notes.front: How does queueing delay grow with utilisation ρ = λ/μ?
notes.back: Roughly as ρ/(1−ρ): flat at low load, explosive near 1. 50% → 90% multiplies the wait ~9×; 90% → 99% another ~10×.
notes.analogy: A motorway: fine at half capacity, stop-and-go at 90%, gridlock just below 100%, with no visible change in the road.
notes.extra: Example: a CPU at 95% looks "efficiently used" on a dashboard; each request waits behind ~19 others.

notes.front: For an M/M/1 queue, what are the average time and number in the system?
notes.back: \(W=\dfrac{1}{\mu-\lambda}=\dfrac{S}{1-\rho}\) and \(L=\dfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\), with service time \(S=1/\mu\).
notes.extra: Example: S = 10 ms, 80 arrivals/s → ρ = 0.8, W = 50 ms. At 95/s → W = 200 ms: +19% load, 4× latency.

notes.text: Kendall notation A/S/c: A = {{c1::arrival process}}, S = {{c2::service-time distribution}}, c = {{c3::number of servers}}. Letters: M = Markovian (Poisson/exponential), G = general, D = deterministic.
notes.extra: Example: a single-threaded worker with Poisson arrivals and wildly varying job sizes is M/G/1, and the "G" is where the pain lives.

notes.front: What does Kingman's formula say about variability and queueing delay?
notes.back: \(W_q\approx\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\cdot\frac{c_a^2+c_s^2}{2}\cdot S\): delay scales with the squared coefficients of variation of inter-arrival and service times, so burstiness and uneven job sizes hurt as much as load.

notes.front: How can you cut queueing delay without adding capacity?
notes.back: Reduce variability: split big jobs or isolate them in their own queue (lower \(c_s\)), and smooth bursty arrivals (lower \(c_a\)).
notes.extra: Example: at 80% utilisation, uniform 10 ms jobs queue far less than a mix of 1 ms and 500 ms jobs.

notes.front: Why are bursts inevitable with Poisson arrivals, even at constant average load?
notes.back: Per-interval counts have variance λ, so intervals well above the average occur routinely. Capacity planned at the average queues constantly; headroom absorbs normal randomness, not just "spikes".

notes.front: One shared queue feeding k servers vs a separate queue per server: which is better, and why?
notes.back: The shared queue: no server idles while another has a backlog, and one slow job blocks one server, not a whole line.
notes.analogy: One snake line feeding six supermarket tills beats six separate lines.
notes.extra: Same reason a single work queue with a worker pool beats per-worker queues, and least-loaded routing beats round-robin to fixed per-instance queues.

notes.front: What is head-of-line blocking?
notes.back: A slow item at the front of a FIFO queue delays everything behind it, even items that could be served instantly.
notes.extra: Shows up in: TCP (one lost packet stalls the stream), HTTP/1.1 pipelining, event loops, ordered Kafka partitions. Fix: per-key ordering with parallelism across keys, or move slow work off the critical path.

notes.front: Why does an overloaded system's throughput often collapse rather than plateau?
notes.back: Queued work still consumes resources, and clients time out and retry, so the effective service rate falls while load rises. Useful throughput drops below what moderate load achieved.

notes.front: How do you prevent congestion collapse?
notes.back: Load shedding, backpressure, bounded queues and retry budgets: drop work early so the rest completes.

notes.front: What does the Universal Scalability Law add to Amdahl's Law?
notes.back: \(X(N)=\frac{N}{1+\alpha(N-1)+\beta N(N-1)}\): besides contention α (the serial part, Amdahl) it adds a coherency cost β (cross-node coordination), so throughput peaks and then falls as N grows.
notes.extra: Example: adding replicas to a strongly consistent database: the 12th node makes everything slower.

notes.front: Fan-out: a page calls 100 backends, each slow 1% of the time. How often is the page slow?
notes.back: \(1-(1-p)^N=1-0.99^{100}\approx\) 63%. The backend p99 becomes the user's p37.

notes.front: How do you mitigate tail latency under fan-out?
notes.back: Hedged requests (send a duplicate after ~p95 delay), tied requests, limiting fan-out, deadline propagation, and reducing backend variance rather than the mean.

notes.front: What does a hypothesis test actually do?
notes.back: It assumes H₀ ("nothing interesting is happening") and asks how surprising data this extreme would be. It can reject H₀ or fail to reject it, never prove it.
notes.extra: Example: A/B test: H₀ = new checkout flow converts the same as old. You observe +2%. The test asks how often random noise alone would produce +2% or more.

notes.front: Define the p-value precisely.
notes.back: \(p=P(\text{statistic at least this extreme}\mid H_0)\). Under H₀, p-values are uniformly distributed on [0, 1].
notes.extra: Example: p = 0.03 for 'new caching layer reduced latency'. It means: if caching did nothing, a gap this large would appear by chance 3% of the time. Whether caching really helps also depends on the prior plausibility and effect size.

notes.front: Name three things a p-value is not.
notes.back: Not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\); not "the probability the result is due to chance" (1 − p is not the chance the effect is real); not a measure of effect size or importance.
notes.extra: Converting to P(H₀ | data) needs a prior and the alternative's likelihood: p = 0.05 often corresponds to a 20–50% posterior probability of the null.

notes.text: Type I error = {{c1::false positive: rejecting a true H₀}}. Type II error = {{c2::false negative: failing to reject a false H₀}}.

notes.front: Why can't you reduce Type I and Type II errors at the same time for free?
notes.back: Tightening the threshold for one loosens the other; only more data or a better test improves both.
notes.extra: Example: Paging threshold: alert on any latency bump → many false pages (Type I). Alert only on huge bumps → missed slow-burn degradations (Type II).

notes.front: What goes wrong when you ignore statistical power?
notes.back: Underpowered studies miss most real effects, and the "significant" effects they do find are inflated (the winner's curse).
notes.extra: Example: an A/B test with 200 users to detect a 1% lift has ~5% power: a null result means nothing and a "win" is almost certainly an exaggerated fluke.

notes.front: What determines statistical power, and how does the required sample size scale with effect size?
notes.back: Power rises with effect size δ, sample size n and α, and falls with noise σ. Required \(n\propto\sigma^2/\delta^2\): halving the detectable effect costs 4× the data.
notes.analogy: Two bell curves (estimate under null and alternative) δ apart: more data doesn't move them, it makes them thinner (width \(\sigma/\sqrt n\)) until they stop overlapping.

notes.front: What does a 95% confidence interval guarantee?
notes.back: A procedure-level guarantee: across repeated experiments, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true value. Not a 95% probability that this particular interval does.
notes.extra: Example: 'Error rate 0.4% (95% CI 0.1%–0.9%)' tells you the data is compatible with anything from 0.1% to 0.9%. A point estimate without an interval hides that the true value could be 9× higher.

notes.front: 95% confidence interval vs 95% credible interval?
notes.back: Confidence: a random interval from a procedure that covers the fixed parameter 95% of the time. Credible: a fixed interval holding 95% posterior probability for the parameter, given this data and prior.
notes.extra: They coincide for flat priors and asymptotically (Bernstein–von Mises), so the misreading usually goes unpunished; they diverge with strong priors, small samples or optional stopping.

notes.front: What is the multiple-comparisons problem, and how do you spot it?
notes.back: Test enough hypotheses and ~5% of true nulls hit p < 0.05 by chance. Spot it: many metrics, subgroups or time windows checked, and only the winners reported.
notes.extra: Example: a dashboard with 40 metrics after a deploy: expect ~2 "significant" regressions with no real change.

notes.front: FWER vs FDR control: what does each limit?
notes.back: FWER: P(at least one false rejection), e.g. Bonferroni (test at α/m); strict, power collapses as m grows. FDR: the expected fraction of rejections that are false, e.g. Benjamini–Hochberg.

notes.front: How does the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure work?
notes.back: Sort the m p-values and reject all up to the largest k with \(p_{(k)}\le\frac{k}{m}\alpha\).
notes.extra: Geometry: null p-values are uniform and hug the diagonal of sorted p vs rank; BH rejects the early p-values that dip too far below a line of slope α/m.

notes.front: What is p-hacking (the garden of forking paths)?
notes.back: Making analysis choices (outliers dropped, metric, stopping time) after seeing the data, so some path reaches significance. Each choice is defensible; the combination guarantees a "finding".

notes.front: Why is "peeking" at an A/B test and stopping once p < 0.05 harmful?
notes.back: Repeated looks give noise many chances to cross the threshold, inflating the false-positive rate to roughly 20–30%.

notes.front: Statistical significance vs practical significance?
notes.back: With enough data, trivially small effects become significant. Ask how big the effect is, with what interval, and whether that size matters.
notes.extra: Example: A change improves p50 latency by 0.3 ms, p < 0.0001, measured on 50 million requests. Significant and irrelevant.

notes.front: What does regression to the mean fool people into believing?
notes.back: That whatever intervention followed an extreme measurement caused the return toward average. Extremes are partly luck and regress even if nothing changed.
notes.extra: Example: You fix the three worst-performing services after a bad week. Next week they improve. Regression to the mean predicts most of that improvement with no fix at all.

notes.front: Statistically, why does regression to the mean happen?
notes.back: In standardised units the regression slope is r with |r| < 1, so a value z SDs from the mean predicts only rz SDs: a property of imperfect correlation, not a causal force.

notes.front: Where does the regression line of y on x sit relative to the data ellipse?
notes.back: Through the points where the ellipse has vertical tangents (midpoints of vertical slices), so it is flatter than the major axis. Regressing x on y gives a steeper line.

notes.front: Why does the sample variance divide by n − 1? (geometric answer)
notes.back: The residual vector \(x-\bar x\mathbf 1\) lies in the (n−1)-dimensional hyperplane orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1\), so noise has only n−1 free coordinates: \(E\|x-\bar x\mathbf 1\|^2=(n-1)\sigma^2\).

notes.text: Degrees of freedom = {{c1::the dimension of the subspace the (residual) vector lives in}}. Fitting p parameters leaves {{c2::n − p}} residual degrees of freedom.
notes.extra: Isotropic noise puts σ² of expected squared length into each dimension.

notes.front: What is the \(\chi^2_k\) distribution geometrically?
notes.back: The squared length of a standard Gaussian vector in k dimensions, \(\sum_{i=1}^kZ_i^2\); mean k, variance 2k.

notes.front: Why does \(\chi^2\) appear everywhere in testing?
notes.back: Test statistics are squared lengths of projections of (roughly) Gaussian noise onto subspaces, and by rotational symmetry only the subspace dimension matters.
notes.extra: Cochran's theorem = Pythagoras for Gaussians: projections onto orthogonal subspaces give independent χ² with df = dimensions.

notes.front: Geometric reading of the F-statistic (e.g. for nested linear models)?
notes.back: \(F=\dfrac{\|P_{\text{signal}}y\|^2/q}{\|P_{\text{resid}}y\|^2/(n-p)}\): squared length per dimension in the extra "signal" subspace vs the residual subspace. Under H₀ both get ≈σ² per dimension, so F ≈ 1.
notes.extra: For nested models the signal subspace is \(V_1\ominus V_0\) (dimension q). \(t^2=F\) when q = 1. A large F: y leans into the extra dimensions more than isotropic noise would.

notes.front: What does the delta method give?
notes.back: If \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)\to N(0,\Sigma)\) and g is differentiable: \(\sqrt n\,(g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta))\to N(0,\nabla g^\top\Sigma\nabla g)\).
notes.extra: Geometry: at scale 1/√n, g looks like its tangent plane, and a linear map of a Gaussian is Gaussian. Fails when ∇g = 0.

notes.front: Why is maximum likelihood estimation a KL projection?
notes.back: Average log-likelihood → \(-H(p^*)-\mathrm{KL}(p^*\|p_\theta)\), so maximising likelihood minimises KL from the data distribution to the model: the KL-closest point on the model manifold.
notes.extra: If the truth is off the model surface (misspecification), MLE converges to the KL-nearest point rather than to nonsense.

notes.front: What are the mean and covariance of the score \(\nabla_\theta\log p(x\mid\theta)\) at the true parameter?
notes.back: Mean 0; covariance = the Fisher information \(I(\theta)\).
notes.analogy: The score is the slope of the log-likelihood hill. At the truth, observations push uphill and downhill with equal expected force; the size of the pushes says how loudly the data speaks about θ.

notes.front: Two equivalent definitions of Fisher information?
notes.back: \(I(\theta)=E[ss^\top]=-E[\nabla^2_\theta\log p(x\mid\theta)]\): variance of the score = expected curvature of the log-likelihood. Independent observations add: \(I_n=nI_1\).
notes.extra: Geometry: a sharply peaked log-likelihood pins θ down; a flat ridge does not. Fisher information is also the Riemannian metric on the model manifold.

notes.front: What does the Cramér–Rao bound say?
notes.back: Any unbiased estimator has \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)\succeq I_n(\theta)^{-1}\) (scalar: \(\mathrm{Var}\ge1/(nI_1)\)): variance ≥ inverse curvature. The MLE attains it asymptotically.

notes.front: What is the asymptotic distribution of the MLE?
notes.back: \(\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N\big(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}\big)\), under regularity conditions.

notes.front: Core idea of the proof that the MLE is asymptotically normal?
notes.back: Taylor-expand the score at \(\theta_0\): the score is a sum (CLT → Gaussian), the Hessian an average (LLN → nI). So \(\hat\theta-\theta_0\approx\) noise / curvature.
notes.extra: Geometry: with lots of data the log-likelihood near its peak is a paraboloid of curvature nI, and a paraboloid log-density is a Gaussian.

notes.text: Likelihood-based tests of \(H_0:\theta=\theta_0\): {{c1::Wald}} uses the horizontal distance \(\hat\theta-\theta_0\) scaled by curvature; {{c2::likelihood ratio}} uses the vertical drop \(2[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta_0)]\); {{c3::score (Lagrange multiplier)}} uses the slope at \(\theta_0\).
notes.extra: All asymptotically χ² and equivalent; they diverge when the log-likelihood isn't quadratic. Wald isn't reparameterisation-invariant (LR is); the score test needs only the null model fitted.

notes.front: What does Wilks' theorem say, and when does it fail?
notes.back: For nested regular models, \(2[\ell(\hat\theta_{\text{full}})-\ell(\hat\theta_{\text{null}})]\to\chi^2_q\) under H₀ (q = constrained parameters). Fails when the null is on the parameter-space boundary (variance = 0, mixture weight = 0).

notes.front: What is a sufficient statistic, and the factorisation criterion?
notes.back: T(x) is sufficient for θ if x given T(x) doesn't depend on θ. Criterion: \(p(x\mid\theta)=g(T(x),\theta)\,h(x)\).
notes.analogy: Lossless compression for inference: which contour of T you land on carries all the information about θ; where you sit within it is pure noise.

notes.front: In an exponential family \(p(x\mid\eta)=h(x)\exp(\eta^\top T(x)-A(\eta))\), what do the derivatives of \(A\) give?
notes.back: \(\nabla A=E[T(x)]\) and \(\nabla^2A=\mathrm{Cov}[T(x)]\). So A is convex, the log-likelihood is concave, and the MLE is moment matching.

notes.front: What is the bootstrap principle?
notes.back: Approximate the population by the empirical distribution and resample the data with replacement; the spread of \(\hat\theta^*\) around \(\hat\theta\) mimics the spread of \(\hat\theta\) around θ.
notes.analogy: We can't rerun "population → sample", so we rerun "sample → resample", which we fully control, and transfer the error distribution back.

notes.front: When does the bootstrap fail?
notes.back: For extremes (max/min), parameters on a boundary, infinite-variance heavy tails, and dependent data unless you resample blocks.

notes.front: What does the Neyman–Pearson lemma say?
notes.back: For simple H₀ vs simple H₁, the most powerful level-α test rejects when the likelihood ratio \(p_1(x)/p_0(x)\) exceeds a threshold.
notes.analogy: A budget of α null-probability to spend on a rejection region: spend it on the points that buy the most alternative probability per unit of null probability (a fractional knapsack).

notes.front: Under model misspecification, what does the MLE converge to, and with what covariance?
notes.back: To the KL-closest ("pseudo-true") parameter, with the sandwich covariance \(A^{-1}BA^{-1}/n\) (A = curvature, B = score variance), which collapses to \(I^{-1}/n\) when the model is correct.

notes.front: What is the James–Stein phenomenon?
notes.back: For \(x\sim N(\theta,I_d)\) with d ≥ 3, shrinking x toward a common point gives lower total mean squared error than the MLE x, for every θ.

notes.front: Geometrically, why does James–Stein shrinkage help?
notes.back: \(E\|x\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+d\): high-dimensional noise is nearly orthogonal to θ, so the observation is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, systematically too long. Shrinking corrects the length.
notes.extra: The root of ridge regression, hierarchical models and empirical Bayes.

notes.front: How does the EM algorithm work, viewed as a lower bound?
notes.back: \(\log p(x\mid\theta)=\mathcal L(q,\theta)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(z\mid x,\theta))\). E-step: set q to the posterior over latents so the bound touches; M-step: maximise the bound over θ. Likelihood never decreases.
notes.analogy: Minorise-maximise: fit a smooth surrogate that lies under the hard curve and touches it, jump to the surrogate's top, repeat.

notes.front: AIC vs BIC: what does each target?
notes.back: AIC \(=-2\ell+2k\) targets prediction (≈ leave-one-out CV; tends to overfit slightly). BIC \(=-2\ell+k\log n\) targets identifying the true model (consistent if it is among the candidates).

notes.front: Describe Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) geometrically.
notes.back: \(\hat y=X\hat\beta\) is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X: minimising squared error = dropping a perpendicular to that plane.
notes.analogy: y floats above the plane spanned by the predictors; the fit is its shadow under a light shining straight down.

notes.front: What do the OLS normal equations say geometrically?
notes.back: \(X^\top(y-X\hat\beta)=0\): the residual is perpendicular to every column of X. Solving gives \(\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\).

notes.text: Hat matrix \(H=X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top\) (\(\hat y=Hy\)): {{c1::symmetric}} (an orthogonal, not oblique, projection), {{c2::idempotent}} (\(H^2=H\)), and its trace = {{c3::rank(X) = p}}, the model degrees of freedom.
notes.extra: Geometry: a projection's eigenvalues are only 1 (kept directions) and 0 (killed); the trace counts the ones. I − H projects onto the (n − p)-dimensional residual space.

notes.front: What is R² geometrically?
notes.back: \(\cos^2\theta\), with θ the angle between the centred response and the centred fitted vector: explained / total squared length in the right triangle.

notes.front: Why does R² never decrease when you add a predictor?
notes.back: A bigger column space can only bring the projection closer to y, even for pure noise (a random column captures ~1/(n−1) of the residual). Adjusted R² corrects for this.

notes.front: Regression's two dual pictures: row picture vs column picture?
notes.back: Row: n points in \(\mathbb R^{p+1}\); fit a hyperplane (good for outliers, leverage, nonlinearity). Column: p predictor vectors and y in \(\mathbb R^n\); project y onto their span (where inference lives).

notes.front: What does the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem say a multiple-regression coefficient means?
notes.back: \(\hat\beta_j\) = the slope from regressing y-residuals on \(x_j\)-residuals (both after removing the other predictors): it uses only the part of \(x_j\) orthogonal to them.
notes.extra: "Controlling for Z" literally means projecting Z out of x and y. If x_j is nearly in the span of the others, the leftover sliver is tiny and the estimate noisy.

notes.front: What is multicollinearity geometrically, and what does it damage?
notes.back: Nearly parallel predictor columns. The fitted \(\hat y\) stays stable, but the coefficients (coordinates in that skewed basis) swing wildly.
notes.analogy: Locating a point with two nearly parallel rulers: a tiny wobble of the point produces huge, offsetting changes in both readings.

notes.front: Define the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF).
notes.back: \(\mathrm{VIF}_j=1/(1-R_j^2)\), with \(R_j^2\) from regressing \(x_j\) on the other predictors; it multiplies \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)\).

notes.front: What does the Gauss–Markov theorem say, and what does it not require?
notes.back: If \(E[\varepsilon]=0\) and \(\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2I\), OLS is BLUE: minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators. Normality is not required.
notes.extra: The class is narrow: biased estimators such as ridge can beat OLS in mean squared error.

notes.front: What is \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\beta)\) for OLS, and what shape is the confidence region?
notes.back: \(\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\): the confidence ellipsoid is the inverse of the data cloud's shape, long where the predictors have little spread.
notes.analogy: A plank on widely spaced supports is stable; on supports bunched together it wobbles.

notes.front: Under what noise model is OLS the MLE, and what do other noise models give?
notes.back: Gaussian noise → squared loss → OLS. Laplace noise → absolute loss (median regression); Student-t → robust regression that downweights outliers.
notes.extra: Rule: the loss is the negative log of the noise density. Squared loss believes in thin tails, so a 10σ outlier is "impossible" and the fit contorts to explain it.

notes.front: What does ridge regression do in the SVD basis of X?
notes.back: \(\hat\beta=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y\) scales the fit along each \(u_j\) by \(d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda)\): high-variance directions barely change, thin (noisy) directions shrink toward 0.
notes.extra: A soft version of principal-component regression, which uses a hard 0/1 cutoff.

notes.front: Why does the lasso (L1) produce exactly-zero coefficients while ridge (L2) does not?
notes.back: The solution is where the elliptical loss contours first touch the constraint ball. The L1 diamond's corners lie on the axes and stick out, so contours usually hit them (coordinates = 0); the round L2 ball has no corners.

notes.text: As MAP estimates under Gaussian noise: ridge = a {{c1::Gaussian}} prior on β; lasso = a {{c2::Laplace (double-exponential)}} prior; λ is a {{c3::noise-to-signal ratio}} (\(\sigma^2/\tau^2\) for ridge).
notes.extra: Penalty = negative log prior. The lasso's zeros are a property of the MAP point only; truly sparse Bayesian answers need spike-and-slab or horseshoe priors.

notes.front: Effective degrees of freedom of a linear smoother, and its value for ridge?
notes.back: \(\mathrm{df}=\mathrm{tr}(S)\); for ridge \(\sum_jd_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda)\), falling from p at λ = 0 to 0 as λ → ∞.

notes.front: What is leverage \(h_{ii}\)?
notes.back: The i-th diagonal of the hat matrix (\(\partial\hat y_i/\partial y_i\)): between 0 and 1, averaging p/n. It depends only on how far \(x_i\) is from the centre of the predictor cloud.

notes.front: What makes a data point influential (Cook's distance)?
notes.back: Large residual × high leverage: \(D_i\propto r_i^2\,h_{ii}/(1-h_{ii})\). A high-leverage point can pull the line onto itself and hide its residual.
notes.analogy: A seesaw: a point far out on the plank tilts the line a lot; an outlier near the fulcrum barely moves it.

notes.front: What breaks under heteroskedasticity?
notes.back: OLS stays unbiased and consistent but is no longer efficient, and the usual standard errors are wrong.

notes.front: Two standard fixes for heteroskedasticity?
notes.back: Keep OLS with robust "sandwich" standard errors, or use GLS: OLS after whitening the noise, so precise observations get more weight.

notes.front: How does the OLS line differ from the first principal component of 2-D data?
notes.back: OLS minimises vertical distances (asymmetric in x and y); PCA minimises perpendicular distances (symmetric; the ellipse's major axis). The OLS line is always flatter.

notes.front: What is attenuation bias?
notes.back: Measurement error in x flattens the OLS slope by the reliability ratio \(\sigma_x^2/(\sigma_x^2+\sigma_{\text{err}}^2)\).

notes.front: When p > n, which interpolating solution do the pseudoinverse and gradient descent from zero pick?
notes.back: The minimum-L2-norm interpolator \(X^+y\). It lies in the row space of X, where gradient descent started at 0 stays forever, since every gradient lies there.
notes.extra: "Ridgeless" regression (λ → 0⁺): the basic mechanism of implicit regularisation.

notes.front: What is the leave-one-out CV shortcut for linear smoothers \(\hat y=Sy\)?
notes.back: \(e_{(i)}=(y_i-\hat y_i)/(1-S_{ii})\): one fit gives all n leave-one-out residuals. GCV replaces \(S_{ii}\) by tr(S)/n.
notes.extra: Removing a point inflates its residual by exactly the factor that undoes its self-influence; high-leverage points flatter themselves most.

notes.text: Generalized Linear Model components: {{c1::random component}} (y from an exponential family: Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, Gamma), {{c2::linear predictor}} \(\eta=X\beta\), and {{c3::link function}} \(g(\mu)=\eta\).
notes.extra: Geometry: the flat plane lives in a warped coordinate system (log-odds, log-rate) chosen so it can never predict an impossible mean.

notes.front: What is special about the canonical link in a GLM?
notes.back: Natural parameter = linear predictor (logit for Bernoulli, log for Poisson, identity for Gaussian). Score equations become \(X^\top(y-\hat\mu)=0\) and the likelihood is concave: residual ⊥ predictors, as in OLS.

notes.front: In logistic regression, what is the geometry of the decision boundary and of w?
notes.back: The boundary p = 0.5 is the hyperplane \(w^\top x+b=0\); w is its normal vector, and ‖w‖ sets how steeply the probability changes away from it.

notes.front: How do you read a logistic-regression coefficient \(w_j\)?
notes.back: \(e^{w_j}\) is the odds ratio per unit increase in \(x_j\) (the log-odds change by \(w_j\)).

notes.front: What happens to logistic regression under perfect separation?
notes.back: The MLE doesn't exist: scaling w up always raises the likelihood, so ‖w‖ → ∞ (huge coefficients and SEs, convergence warnings). Fix: L1/L2 penalty, Firth correction, weakly informative priors.

notes.front: How is a GLM fitted?
notes.back: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares: Newton/Fisher scoring where each step solves a weighted least-squares problem on a working response, re-linearising around the current fit.
notes.extra: \(\beta^{\text{new}}=(X^\top WX)^{-1}X^\top Wz\), \(z=\eta+(y-\mu)g'(\mu)\), \(W=1/(V(\mu)g'(\mu)^2)\).

notes.front: What is deviance in a GLM?
notes.back: \(D=2[\ell_{\text{saturated}}-\ell_{\text{fitted}}]\): the GLM's analogue of the residual sum of squares (RSS/σ² for Gaussian). Deviance differences between nested models are LR statistics, ≈ χ².

notes.front: What is overdispersion in count models, and its symptom?
notes.back: Real counts have Var(y) > μ, which Poisson forbids. Coefficients stay roughly fine but standard errors are too small. Diagnostic: residual deviance / df ≫ 1.

notes.front: Fixes for overdispersion?
notes.back: Quasi-Poisson (estimate a dispersion factor), Negative Binomial (\(\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\mu^2/k\)), or observation-level random effects.
notes.extra: The Negative Binomial is a Poisson with a Gamma-distributed rate; mixing always adds variance (law of total variance).

notes.front: What is partial pooling in a hierarchical (mixed-effects) model?
notes.back: Group effects are drawn from a common distribution, so each group's estimate is a precision-weighted compromise between its own mean and the grand mean; small or noisy groups shrink most.
notes.analogy: A slider between "no pooling" (each group alone: high variance) and "complete pooling" (one mean for all: high bias); the data set the slider.

notes.front: Shrinkage formula for a group mean in a hierarchical model?
notes.back: \(\hat\alpha_j=\lambda_j\bar y_j+(1-\lambda_j)\hat\mu\), with \(\lambda_j=\dfrac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2/n_j}\).
notes.extra: It is James–Stein with the amount of shrinkage learned from the data.

notes.front: How do smoothing splines / GAMs fit nonlinear functions while remaining linear models?
notes.back: Expand x in a basis (B-splines) and penalise roughness \(\lambda\int f''(x)^2dx=\lambda\beta^\top\Omega\beta\): generalised ridge regression, with λ chosen by CV or REML.
notes.extra: Geometry: the straight-line part is untouched; wigglier basis directions are shrunk progressively harder, like a low-pass filter.

notes.front: In kernel / local regression, what does the bandwidth h control?
notes.back: The bias–variance trade-off: small h → wiggly fit (low bias, high variance); large h → flat fit (high bias, low variance).

notes.front: How does the best achievable kernel-regression error rate degrade with dimension?
notes.back: From \(n^{-4/5}\) in 1-D to \(n^{-4/(4+d)}\) in d dimensions: the curse of dimensionality stated as a theorem.

notes.front: In survival analysis, what is the hazard function?
notes.back: The instantaneous failure rate among survivors: \(h(t)=\lim_{dt\to0}P(t\le T<t+dt\mid T\ge t)/dt\).

notes.front: How does the Cox model handle censoring without specifying a baseline hazard?
notes.back: Partial likelihood: at each event time, a softmax of \(e^{x^\top\beta}\) over the current risk set, so \(h_0(t)\) cancels. Censored subjects count in risk sets until they drop out.

notes.front: What loss does quantile regression minimise, and why does it give a quantile?
notes.back: The pinball loss: under-predictions cost τ per unit, over-predictions 1 − τ. At the minimum a fraction τ of the data lies below the prediction (τ = 0.5 → median).
notes.analogy: A tilted V: squared loss balances like a centre of mass (mean), absolute loss by head-count (median); tilting the V moves the balance point to any quantile, e.g. a p99 latency model.

notes.text: Explanations for an observed correlation between X and Y: {{c1::X causes Y}}; {{c2::Y causes X (reverse causation)}}; {{c3::a third variable Z causes both (confounding)}}; plus chance and selection effects.
notes.extra: Example: Services with more monitoring have more incidents. Monitoring causes incidents? No: important services get both more monitoring and more scrutiny (confounder), and incidents lead to more monitoring (reverse).

notes.front: How does randomisation deal with confounders?
notes.back: Random assignment breaks any link between confounders and treatment, so the remaining outcome difference is causal (in expectation).
notes.extra: Example: Users who enable dark mode retain better. Confounder: engaged power users both enable dark mode and retain. Randomly forcing dark mode on for half of new users removes that link.

notes.front: Causal adjustment: should you adjust for a confounder \(X\leftarrow Z\rightarrow Y\)?
notes.back: Yes: it opens a spurious back-door path between X and Y.

notes.front: Should you adjust for a mediator \(X\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\)?
notes.back: Not if you want the total effect: adjusting blocks the part of the effect that flows through M.

notes.front: What is a collider (\(X\rightarrow C\leftarrow Y\)), and why must you not condition on it?
notes.back: A variable caused by both X and Y. Conditioning or selecting on it creates a spurious X–Y association (Berkson's paradox).
notes.analogy: Talent and looks are unrelated in the population, but among people who became actors (talent + looks above a bar) they look negatively correlated.
notes.extra: Example: Among hired candidates, coding-test score and interview charm are negatively correlated—because hiring required being strong in at least one. In the applicant pool they are unrelated.

notes.front: Confounder vs collider: what does adjusting for each do to a spurious association?
notes.back: Adjusting for a confounder removes a spurious association; adjusting for a collider creates one.

notes.front: Selection bias vs survivorship bias?
notes.back: Selection bias: the sample is unrepresentative because of how it was chosen. Survivorship bias: you only see cases that made it through some filter.
notes.extra: Example: WWII bombers returned with bullet holes on wings and fuselage; the fix was to armor the engines—the places with no holes, because planes hit there never came back. Postmortems only cover incidents that got noticed.

notes.front: What is Simpson's paradox?
notes.back: A trend in every subgroup reverses when groups are pooled, because group membership is associated with both x and y (e.g. group sizes differ across the comparison).
notes.analogy: Several small clouds each tilting upward, stacked in a staircase that goes down: the pooled fit follows the staircase.
notes.extra: Example: Cluster A has a lower error rate than cluster B for both small requests and large requests. Yet A's overall error rate is higher, because A handles mostly large (error-prone) requests. Aggregates without stratification lie. Which slope is "right" is a causal question (confounder or collider?), not a statistical one.

notes.front: What is the counterfactual definition of a causal effect, and why is it unobservable?
notes.back: Effect on unit i = \(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\). Only one of the two outcomes ever happens: the fundamental problem of causal inference.
notes.extra: Example: Did the migration reduce cost? The counterfactual is the cost this quarter had you not migrated—which you never observe. Comparing to last quarter assumes nothing else changed.

notes.front: The naive treated-vs-control difference = ATE + what?
notes.back: Selection bias: \(E[Y(0)\mid T=1]-E[Y(0)\mid T=0]\). Randomisation makes treatment independent of potential outcomes, so this term is zero.

notes.front: What must hold to identify the ATE from observational data?
notes.back: Conditional ignorability \(T\perp Y(t)\mid X\) (no unmeasured confounders) and overlap \(0

notes.front: What is a propensity score, and why is adjusting for it alone enough?
notes.back: \(e(x)=P(T=1\mid X=x)\). If treatment is ignorable given X, it is ignorable given e(X): within a propensity stratum, treatment is as good as a coin flip.

notes.front: How does inverse probability weighting use the propensity score, and where does it break?
notes.back: Weight treated units by 1/e and controls by 1/(1 − e). Weights explode near e = 0 or 1: regions without overlap, where the data can't speak.

notes.front: Difference-in-differences: what assumption does it rely on?
notes.back: Parallel trends: absent treatment, treated and control groups would have moved in parallel.
notes.extra: Example: Diff-in-diff: region EU got the new autoscaler, US did not. Compare EU's before/after change to US's before/after change, which nets out the global traffic trend.

notes.front: What problem do instrumental variables solve, and what must an instrument satisfy?
notes.back: A regressor correlated with the error (confounding, reverse causation, measurement error) makes OLS inconsistent. The instrument must be relevant (moves x) and excluded (affects y only through x).

notes.front: What does Two-Stage Least Squares do geometrically?
notes.back: Projects x onto the instrument's span (the clean part, orthogonal to the error), then regresses y on that projection. A weak instrument leaves a tiny sliver: noisy and biased toward OLS.

notes.front: Regression discontinuity: what assumption does it rely on?
notes.back: Units just above and just below a cutoff are comparable, so the jump in outcome at the cutoff is the causal effect.

notes.front: Why does "we changed X and metric Y improved" prove little?
notes.back: Before/after comparisons are confounded by everything else that changed (traffic, other deploys, seasonality) and by regression to the mean.

notes.front: How can you strengthen a before/after causal claim?
notes.back: A concurrent control or randomisation, a dose–response pattern, or a reversal test: turn the change off on half the fleet and see whether Y degrades.
notes.extra: Example: Latency improved after the JVM flag change—during the weekend traffic dip. Turn the flag off on half the fleet on Monday and compare.

notes.front: State the omitted variable bias formula and what bias requires.
notes.back: \(E[\hat\beta_{\text{short}}]=\beta+\gamma\delta\). Bias needs both: z affects y (γ ≠ 0) and z correlates with x (δ ≠ 0).
notes.extra: Geometry: the part of z parallel to x gets projected onto x and credited to it; only a z perpendicular to x falls harmlessly into the residual.

notes.text: Bayes' theorem \(P(H\mid E)=\dfrac{P(E\mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}\): \(P(H)\) is the {{c1::prior}} (belief before evidence); \(P(E\mid H)\) the {{c2::likelihood}} (how expected E is if H is true); \(P(E)\) the {{c3::evidence / marginal}} (how expected E is overall); \(P(H\mid E)\) the {{c4::posterior}}.
notes.extra: Example: An alert fires (E). How likely is a real outage (H)? Depends on how often outages happen (prior), how reliably the alert fires during outages (likelihood), and how often the alert fires at all, including false alarms (evidence).

notes.front: Base-rate neglect: a 99%-accurate test for a disease 1 in 10,000 people have. You test positive. Roughly how likely is it you have it?
notes.back: About 1%. Per million people: ~99 true positives vs ~9,999 false positives. An extreme prior dominates.
notes.extra: Example: An anomaly detector with a 1% false-positive rate on 100,000 daily requests produces ~1,000 false alarms a day. Even if it catches every real attack, most alerts are noise when real attacks are rare.

notes.front: What is a likelihood ratio, and the odds form of Bayes?
notes.back: \(LR=P(E\mid H)/P(E\mid\neg H)\); posterior odds = prior odds × LR. Evidence with LR ≈ 1 is uninformative, however dramatic it feels.
notes.extra: Example: 'The service was deployed yesterday' as evidence for 'the deploy caused the incident': if deploys happen daily, P(deployed yesterday) is ~1 under both hypotheses, so LR ≈ 1 and it barely moves you.

notes.front: Why is "extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence" just Bayes?
notes.back: A tiny prior needs a huge likelihood ratio to reach a high posterior; ordinary evidence (LR 2–10) can't lift a 1-in-a-million prior to credible.
notes.extra: Example: A paper claims a 10× speedup from a trivial config change. Prior: such free wins are rare. You need strong, reproducible evidence, not one benchmark chart.

notes.front: Geometrically, what does a Bayesian update do?
notes.back: Multiplies prior and likelihood pointwise over parameter space and renormalises: the posterior is high only where both are high (log-posterior = log-likelihood + log-prior + const).

notes.front: Normal prior, normal likelihood (known variance): what are the posterior precision and mean?
notes.back: Precisions add: \(1/\tau_n^2=1/\tau_0^2+n/\sigma^2\). The mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean \(\mu_0\) and the data mean \(\bar x\), nearer the sharper one.
notes.analogy: A centre of mass: weights at the prior mean and the data mean, with masses equal to their precisions. As n grows the data's mass dominates and the prior is forgotten.

notes.front: What is a conjugate prior? Give the Beta-Binomial update.
notes.back: A prior family closed under the likelihood's update. Beta(a, b) + k successes in n trials → Beta(a + k, b + n − k).
notes.analogy: The hyperparameters are pseudo-counts: the prior acts like a + b imaginary earlier trials.

notes.front: Beta-Binomial: why is the posterior mean a compromise?
notes.back: \(\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\) is a weighted average of the prior mean \(\frac{a}{a+b}\) and the sample proportion \(\frac kn\), with weights a + b and n.

notes.front: Posterior predictive vs plug-in prediction?
notes.back: \(p(\tilde x\mid x)=\int p(\tilde x\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\) averages over parameter uncertainty, so it is wider than plugging in \(\hat\theta\) (Normal: variance \(\sigma^2+\tau_n^2\)).
notes.extra: Aleatoric noise plus epistemic (parameter) uncertainty; only the second shrinks with data.

notes.front: How does the marginal likelihood (evidence) implement an automatic Occam's razor?
notes.back: \(p(x\mid M)\) is the probability the model gave the data before seeing it. A flexible model spreads its mass over many possible datasets; a simple model that fits concentrates its mass and wins.
notes.extra: Laplace view: evidence ≈ best-fit likelihood × (posterior volume / prior volume); the second factor is the Occam penalty.

notes.front: What is a Bayes factor?
notes.back: \(BF_{10}=p(x\mid M_1)/p(x\mid M_0)\); posterior odds = Bayes factor × prior odds.

notes.front: What is the Jeffreys–Lindley paradox?
notes.back: With a point null and a diffuse prior under the alternative, a small p-value can coexist with a Bayes factor strongly favouring the null, increasingly so as n grows or the prior widens.
notes.extra: A very wide prior wastes its mass far from the data. Unlike posteriors, Bayes factors never forget the prior.

notes.front: What does the Bernstein–von Mises theorem say?
notes.back: Under regularity (fixed dimension, prior positive at the truth, correct model) the posterior → \(N(\hat\theta_{MLE},I(\theta_0)^{-1}/n)\): the prior washes out and credible sets become valid confidence sets.
notes.extra: Fails when dimension grows with n, in nonparametric models, at boundaries, and under misspecification.

notes.text: Bayes point estimates: the posterior mean minimises {{c1::squared error}}; the median minimises {{c2::absolute error}}; the mode (MAP) minimises {{c3::0–1 loss}} (in the limit).

notes.front: What is the conceptual weakness of the MAP estimate?
notes.back: It is not invariant to reparameterisation (densities transform with a Jacobian, so the peak moves when you change coordinates), and it ignores posterior mass.
notes.extra: Mass is real; height is a coordinate artefact. In high dimensions the mode can sit where there is negligible mass.

notes.front: What is the Jeffreys prior, and its key property?
notes.back: \(p(\theta)\propto\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}\): invariant under reparameterisation, i.e. uniform on the statistical manifold measured with the Fisher metric. Bernoulli → Beta(½, ½).

notes.front: What does de Finetti's theorem say?
notes.back: An infinite exchangeable (order-invariant) sequence is a mixture of i.i.d. sequences: if order doesn't matter to you, you are acting as if there is an unknown parameter with a prior.

notes.front: What is empirical Bayes?
notes.back: Estimate the prior's hyperparameters from the data by maximising the marginal likelihood, then compute posteriors as usual. Units borrow strength from each other; it understates uncertainty.
notes.extra: James–Stein is empirical Bayes for the Normal-means problem.

notes.front: What is the Bayes-optimal decision?
notes.back: The action minimising posterior expected loss \(\int L(\theta,a)\,p(\theta\mid x)\,d\theta\). Inference and decision separate: one posterior serves any loss.
notes.extra: With asymmetric loss (overstock cheap, stockout costly) the optimal action is a quantile, not the mean.

notes.front: Prior vs posterior predictive checks?
notes.back: Prior predictive: simulate data from the prior alone to catch priors implying absurd observables. Posterior predictive: simulate replicated data from the fit and compare a test statistic with the observed one to reveal misfit.

notes.front: Why does the typical set matter for Bayesian computation?
notes.back: In high dimensions almost all posterior mass lies in a thin shell away from the mode, so expectations come from that shell: MAP optimisation finds an atypical point, and samplers must explore the shell.

notes.front: What is the Laplace approximation?
notes.back: A Gaussian at the MAP with covariance = inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior: \(N(\hat\theta_{MAP},H^{-1})\). Purely local; poor for skewed, multimodal or boundary posteriors.

notes.front: How does Metropolis–Hastings work?
notes.back: Propose θ′ from q; accept with probability \(\min\!\big(1,\frac{p(\theta')q(\theta\mid\theta')}{p(\theta)q(\theta'\mid\theta)}\big)\), else stay. Only density ratios are needed, so the normaliser cancels.
notes.analogy: A hiker who always takes uphill steps and takes downhill steps with probability equal to the height ratio: time spent at each spot becomes proportional to its height.

notes.front: Why does Metropolis–Hastings target the right distribution?
notes.back: The acceptance rule enforces detailed balance \(p(\theta)T(\theta\to\theta')=p(\theta')T(\theta'\to\theta)\), which makes p the stationary distribution.

notes.front: What is Gibbs sampling, and when does it mix badly?
notes.back: Draw each coordinate (or block) from its full conditional in turn: Metropolis–Hastings with acceptance 1. Mixes badly when parameters are strongly correlated: axis-aligned steps crawl along a diagonal ridge.

notes.front: How does Hamiltonian Monte Carlo work, and why does it scale?
notes.back: Add a momentum variable, simulate Hamiltonian dynamics with the leapfrog integrator (using \(\nabla\log p\)), then Metropolis-accept. Energy is nearly conserved, so distant proposals are accepted.
notes.analogy: A frictionless puck flicked across the negative-log-posterior surface: it glides along the valley's contours instead of stumbling randomly.
notes.extra: Cost per independent draw ~d^(5/4) vs d² for random walk. NUTS picks trajectory length automatically.

notes.front: What is Neal's funnel?
notes.back: In hierarchical models (\(\alpha_j\sim N(\mu,\tau)\)), small τ squeezes the α's together and large τ frees them: curvature varies by orders of magnitude, no single step size works, and HMC reports divergences.

notes.front: How does the non-centred parameterisation fix the funnel, and when should you use it?
notes.back: Sample \(z_j\sim N(0,1)\) and set \(\alpha_j=\mu+\tau z_j\): the funnel straightens into a near-isotropic blob. Use it when data per group is weak.

notes.text: MCMC diagnostics: {{c1::\(\hat R\)}} compares between- and within-chain variance (want < 1.01); {{c2::effective sample size (ESS)}} counts equivalent independent draws; {{c3::divergences}} (HMC) mean estimates are biased, not merely noisy.
notes.extra: R-hat can only detect non-convergence, never prove convergence.

notes.front: What does variational inference optimise?
notes.back: It picks q from a tractable family to minimise \(\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(\theta\mid x))\), by maximising the ELBO, since \(\log p(x)=\mathrm{ELBO}(q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(\theta\mid x))\).
notes.extra: Fast and scalable, but biased by the family's shape; mean-field typically underestimates variance.

notes.front: Reverse KL(q‖p) vs forward KL(p‖q) when fitting a unimodal q to a multimodal p?
notes.back: Reverse (variational inference): mode-seeking, locks onto one mode, too narrow. Forward (maximum likelihood, EP): mass-covering, straddles all modes and puts mass in the empty valley between them.
notes.extra: Geometry: the expectation is under the first argument. Under q you never look where q is zero, so ignoring a mode is free; under p you are inspected everywhere p lives.

notes.front: What is a Gaussian Process?
notes.back: A distribution over functions in which any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian, specified by a mean function and a kernel \(k(x,x')\) that says how strongly nearby values are tied.

notes.front: How does GP regression predict, and what does it cost?
notes.back: By Gaussian conditioning on the observed points: mean \(k_*^\top(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}y\); the variance pinches near the data and returns to the prior far away. Cost \(O(n^3)\).

notes.front: How are Bayesian linear regression, ridge, kernel ridge and GP regression related?
notes.back: Bayesian linear regression with prior \(N(0,\tau^2I)\) has posterior mean = ridge (λ = σ²/τ²). Swapping x for features φ(x) induces a kernel; the GP posterior mean = kernel ridge, plus a predictive variance.

notes.front: How does importance sampling work?
notes.back: \(E_p[f]=E_q[f\,p/q]\): sample from q and reweight by \(w=p/q\). q needs heavier tails than p.

notes.front: Why does importance sampling break down in high dimensions?
notes.back: Weight variance grows exponentially with d: the typical sets of p and q barely overlap, so one sample carries nearly all the weight.
